ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
A capacitor with capacitance \( C \) is connected to a variable electromotive force DC power supply through the left side of a single-pole double-throw switch \( S \), and to two smooth horizontal metal rails \( M_1M_2P_1P_2 \) and \( N_1N_2Q_1Q_2 \) with a spacing of \( L \) on the right side (a small section of smooth insulating material is placed at \( M_1 \) on the left side, and all parts are smoothly connected). The horizontal rails have two regions with uniform magnetic fields of magnitude \( B \), where region I has a vertically upward direction and region II has a vertically downward direction. The width between the dashed lines is \( d \), and the distance between the two regions is sufficiently large. Two metal rods \( a \) and \( b \), each with resistance \( R \), are placed perpendicular to the rails. Rod \( a \) has a mass \( m \), and rod \( b \) has a mass \( 3m \). Rod \( b \) is placed at the midpoint \( EF \) of magnetic field region II and is tied with an insulating thread, which can withstand a maximum tension of \( F_0 \). Now, switch \( S \) is thrown to position "1", and after sufficient time, it is thrown to position "2". It is known that rod \( a \) has already reached a steady-state motion before arriving at the small section of insulating material.

1. After rod a slides over the insulating material, if rod b is to remain stationary on the rails, should the electromotive force of the power supply be less than a certain value \( E_0 \)? What is the magnitude of \( E_0 \)?
2. If the electromotive force of the power supply is less than \( E_0 \), causing rod \( a \) to slide over the insulating material at a speed \( v_1 \) (where \( v_1 \) is a known quantity), what is the Joule heat generated by rod \( a \) as it passes through the dashed lines \( M_1N_1 \) and \( M_2N_2 \)?
3. If the electromotive force of the power supply is greater than \( E_0 \), causing rod \( a \) to slide over the insulating material at a speed \( v_2 \) (where \( v_2 \) is a known quantity), and timing starts from the moment rod \( a \) just slides over the insulating material, after a time \( t_0 \), it slides past the dashed line \( M_2N_2 \), at which point the speed of rod \( a \) is \( \frac{1}{2} v_2 \). What is the speed of metal rod \( b \) at time \( t_0 \)?

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The attached figure shows a variable power supply E, capacitor C, and single-pole double-throw switch S on the left; when the switch is connected to the right side, it is connected into two smooth horizontal parallel rails. The spacing between the rails is marked as L. In the left magnetic-field region I there is a vertically upward B arrow, and metal rod a perpendicularly spans the rails; at the right end of region I there are two blue dashed lines M1N1 and M2N2, with the spacing marked as d. Farther to the right is magnetic-field region II, with the B arrow vertically downward, and metal rod b is located in it and spans the upper and lower rails, with an EF midpoint mark beside it. The spacing between the dashed lines P1Q1 and P2Q2 of region II is also marked as d, and there is a fixed end at the right end indicating the constraint of a light string. Reasoning: First make the switch connect to position 1; after sufficiently long, the capacitor voltage is E. Then connect to position 2; rod a is accelerated by the Ampere force in the magnetic field, and has already reached a steady state before reaching the small insulating segment. Let this steady-state velocity be vs. During the acceleration process m dv/dt = B L i; in steady state, the circuit current is 0, so the remaining capacitor voltage is equal to the motional electromotive force B L vs of rod a. The capacitor discharge amount is C(E − B L vs). Integrating the impulse of the Ampere force: m vs = B L · C(E − B L vs), so vs = C B L E / (m + C B²L²). 1. After rod a slides over the small insulating segment, if rod b is still fixed, then the resistances of the two rods are in series, the total resistance is 2R, and the motional electromotive force of rod a produces current I = B L vs/(2R). The magnitude of the magnetic force on rod b is F = B L I = B²L² vs/(2R). To make the light string not break and rod b remain stationary, there should be F ≤ F0. Substituting vs gives E ≤ 2R F0(m + C B²L²)/(C B³L³), and the critical value E0 = 2R F0(m + C B²L²)/(C B³L³). Therefore it should be less than or not exceed this critical value. 2. When E < E0, rod b does not move. Rod a enters the width d region from M1N1 to M2N2 with v1, the current I = B L v/(2R), and rod a is subjected to resistance B L I, so m dv/dt = −B²L² v/(2R). Also dx/dt = v, so dv/dx = −B²L²/(2mR). After passing through distance d, v_out = v1 − B²L²d/(2mR). The Joule heat on rod a is Qa = ∫ I²R dt = ∫ [B²L² v²/(4R)] dt = B²L²/(4R) ∫ v dx. Since v varies linearly with x, ∫ v dx = d(v1 + v_out)/2, so Qa = B²L²d/(8R)·(2v1 − B²L²d/(2mR)). 3. When E > E0, the light string cannot keep rod b stationary, and afterward the two rods move coupled through electromagnetic action. According to the problem statement, starting from just after rod a passes the small insulating segment, the initial state is va = v2, vb = 0; during motion, m dva/dt = −B L I, 3m dvb/dt = B L I. Adding the two equations gives d(m va + 3m vb)/dt = 0, that is, va + 3vb = v2. At t0, va = v2/2, so v2/2 + 3vb = v2, solving gives vb = v2/6.
